claim: BUB-1 is a protein of the Spindle Assembly Checkpoint (SAC) that coordinates chromosome attachment with anaphase onset.
source: BUB-1 is a protein of the Spindle Assembly Checkpoint (SAC) that coordinates chromosome attachment with anaphase onset.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: BUB-1 is required for accurate sister chromatid segregation independently of its SAC function.
source: BUB-1 is also required for accurate sister chromatid segregation independently of its SAC function, but the underlying mechanism remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data and citations in the introduction.

claim: In C. elegans embryos, BUB-1 accelerates the establishment of non-merotelic end-on kinetochore-microtubule attachments by recruiting the RZZ complex and its downstream partner dynein-dynactin at the kinetochore.
source: Here we show that, in Caenorhabditis elegans embryos, BUB-1 accelerates the establishment of non-merotelic end-on kinetochore-microtubule attachments by recruiting the RZZ complex and its downstream partner dynein-dynactin at the kinetochore.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: BUB-1 limits attachment maturation by the SKA complex.
source: In parallel, BUB-1 limits attachment maturation by the SKA complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: BUB-1 activity opposes kinetochore-microtubule attachment stabilisation promoted by CLS-2CLASP-dependent kinetochore-microtubule assembly.
source: This activity opposes kinetochore-microtubule attachment stabilisation promoted by CLS-2CLASP-dependent kinetochore-microtubule assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing rescue of chromosome biorientation upon co-depletion of BUB-1 and CLS-2CLASP.

claim: The NDC80 complex and the Rod-Zw10-Zwilch (RZZ)-Spindly kinetochore module are two main kinetochore microtubule-binding modules in metazoans.
source: In metazoans, two main kinetochore microtubule-binding modules ensure efficient interaction with spindle microtubules: the NDC80 complex and the Rod-Zw10-Zwilch (RZZ)-Spindly kinetochore module that recruits dynein-dynactin motors to kinetochores (Gassmann et al., 2008a; Griffis et al., 2007; Scaërou et al., 1999; Starr et al., 1998; Williams et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: The NDC80 complex interacts with microtubule plus-ends to establish load-bearing end-coupled connections between kinetochores and the mitotic spindle.
source: The NDC80 complex interacts with microtubule plus-ends to establish load-bearing end-coupled connections between kinetochores and the mitotic spindle (Cheeseman et al., 2006; DeLuca et al., 2005; McCleland et al., 2003; Wigge and Kilmartin, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Kinetochore-localized dynein mediates initial lateral capture of microtubules to ensure correct kinetochore orientation.
source: Kinetochore-localized dynein mediates initial lateral capture of microtubules to ensure correct kinetochore orientation (Gassmann et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Initial kinetochore orientation limits merotelic connections and accelerates formation of NDC80-mediated end-coupled attachments.
source: This initial kinetochore orientation limits merotelic connections, where individual kinetochores are attached to both spindle poles, and accelerates formation of NDC80-mediated end-coupled attachments (Rieder and Alexander, 1990; Rieder and Salmon, 1998; Varma et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The RZZ complex inhibits NDC80 binding to microtubules until dynein has properly oriented kinetochores.
source: The transition from initial lateral to load-bearing end-coupled attachments is coordinated by the RZZ complex itself, which inhibits NDC80 binding to microtubules until dynein has properly oriented kinetochores (Cheerambathur et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The SKA complex interacts with NDC80 and kinetochore microtubules to reinforce load-bearing connections.
source: Once properly established, load-bearing connections are subsequently reinforced by the SKA complex, which interacts with NDC80 and kinetochore microtubules (Auckland et al., 2017; Cheerambathur et al., 2017; Gaitanos et al., 2009; Helgeson et al., 2018; Janczyk et al., 2017; Schmidt et al., 2012; Theis et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: BUB1 was originally identified as a component of the Spindle Assembly Checkpoint (SAC).
source: An additional key player in the process of chromosome alignment is the kinetochore BUB1 kinase that was originally identified as a component of the Spindle Assembly Checkpoint (SAC), a mechanism that delays anaphase onset until all kinetochores are properly connected to the spindle (reviewed in Joglekar, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: BUB1 is essential to preserve ploidy throughout mitosis in budding and fission yeasts independently of the SAC.
source: Indeed, independently of the SAC, BUB1 was shown to be essential to preserve ploidy throughout mitosis in budding and fission yeasts (Bernard et al., 1998; Vanoosthuyse et al., 2004; Warren et al., 2002)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: BUB1 promotes chromosome alignment and accurate segregation essential for embryonic development in C. elegans oocytes and embryos.
source: to promote chromosome alignment and accurate segregation essential for embryonic development in C. elegans oocytes and embryos (Essex et al., 2009; Laband et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: BUB1 ensures efficient chromosome congression and segregation and prevents aneuploidy in human tissue cultured cells.
source: and to ensure efficient chromosome congression and segregation and prevent aneuploidy in human tissue cultured cells (Johnson et al., 2004; Klebig et al., 2009; Meraldi and Sorger, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: BUB1 phosphorylation of histone H2A and subsequent recruitment of Shugoshin target protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) and Aurora B kinase to the inner centromere.
source: BUB1 phosphorylation of histone H2A (Kawashima et al., 2010; Ricke et al., 2012) and subsequent recruitment of the centromeric protein Shugoshin (Fernius and Hardwick, 2007) target protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) and Aurora B kinase to the inner centromere (Kawashima et al., 2010; Yamagishi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: BUB1 interacts with BUBR1, which leads to kinetochore recruitment of PP2A.
source: In parallel, BUB1 interacts with BUBR1, which leads to kinetochore recruitment of PP2A (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Several studies suggest that BUB1 can regulate kinetochore-microtubule attachment independently of the Aurora B/PP2A pathway.
source: However, several studies suggest that BUB1 can regulate kinetochore-microtubule attachment independently of this pathway (Johnson et al., 2004; Meraldi and Sorger, 2005; Perera and Taylor, 2010; Raaijmakers et al., 2018; Windecker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: BUB1 recruits CENP-F via its kinase domain but independently of kinase activity.
source: A second function of BUB1 that could account for its role in regulating kinetochore-microtubule attachments is the recruitment of the kinetochore protein CENP-F, via its kinase domain but independently of kinase activity (Berto et al., 2018; Ciossani et al., 2018; Encalada et al., 2005; Johnson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: BUB1 contributes to recruiting the RZZ complex to kinetochores in human cells.
source: Alternatively, as BUB1 contributes to recruiting the RZZ complex to kinetochores in human cells (Caldas et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The loss of BUB1-dependent kinetochore targeting of the RZZ complex is not sufficient to account for the lethality of SAC-deficient haploid (HAP1) cells upon BUB1 depletion.
source: Yet, the loss of BUB1-dependent kinetochore targeting of the RZZ complex is not sufficient to account for the lethality of SAC-deficient haploid (HAP1) cells upon BUB1 depletion (Raaijmakers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: In control C. elegans zygotes, progressive chromosome congression leads to the formation of a tight metaphase plate.
source: In control zygotes, progressive chromosome congression led to the formation of a tight metaphase plate (Figure 1B,C; Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1B,C and Video 1.

claim: In control zygotes, slow spindle pole separation occurs from 80 s after NEBD until anaphase onset at 140 s after NEBD.
source: This correlated with slow spindle pole separation from 80 s after nuclear envelope breakdown (NEBD) until anaphase onset (140 s after NEBD), and was followed by sister chromatid segregation concomitant with fast spindle pole separation (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: In BUB-1-depleted zygotes, anaphase onset is delayed compared to controls (around 200 s after NEBD).
source: In BUB-1-depleted zygotes, anaphase onset was delayed compared to controls (around 200 s after NEBD, Figure 1B,C)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: BUB-1 promotes anaphase onset through Cdc20 activation.
source: in agreement with BUB-1 promoting anaphase onset through Cdc20 activation (Kim et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: In BUB-1-depleted zygotes, a chromosome congression pause coincides with a 'bump' in the pole separation profile.
source: In these embryos, a chromosome congression pause was visible in the kymographs, as evidenced by a constant chromosome span that coincided with a previously described 'bump' in the pole separation profile (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The spindle pole bump in BUB-1-depleted zygotes reflects delayed load-bearing attachments.
source: This spindle pole bump has been shown to reflect delayed load-bearing attachments (Kim et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Bent kinetochores during metaphase and kinetochore stretches during anaphase in BUB-1-depleted zygotes indicate merotelic connections.
source: Instead, bent kinetochores during metaphase and kinetochore stretches during anaphase were visible in BUB-1-depleted zygotes, which in holocentric embryos indicate merotelic connections of individual kinetochores to both spindle poles (Figure 1F–H) (Essex et al., 2009; Maton et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations and shown in Figure 1F-H.

claim: BUB-1 depletion delays load-bearing attachments, leading to a lag in chromosome congression, followed by the establishment of merotelic attachments.
source: BUB-1 depletion therefore delays load-bearing attachments, leading to a lag in chromosome congression, followed by the establishment of merotelic attachments to both spindle poles.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1 is required for kinetochore recruitment of HCP-1 and HCP-2.
source: BUB-1 is required for kinetochore recruitment of the two redundant CENP-F orthologs HCP-1 and 2, which in turn recruit CLS-2CLASP (Figure 1D) (Cheeseman et al., 2005; Maton et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations and shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: HCP-1/2CENP-F recruit CLS-2CLASP to kinetochores.
source: BUB-1 is required for kinetochore recruitment of the two redundant CENP-F orthologs HCP-1 and 2, which in turn recruit CLS-2CLASP (Figure 1D) (Cheeseman et al., 2005; Maton et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations and shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: GFP-tagged HCP-1CENP-F, HCP-2CENP-F, and CLS-2CLASP are absent from kinetochores upon BUB-1 depletion.
source: We imaged C. elegans zygotes expressing endogenous GFP-tagged HCP-1CENP-F or HCP-2CENP-F, or a GFP-tagged CLS-2CLASP transgene, and confirmed their absence from kinetochores upon BUB-1 depletion (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Following depletion of HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP, chromosomes do not congress, and chromosomes and spindle poles separate prematurely 40 s after NEBD concomitant with sister chromatid co-segregation.
source: In line with previous observations, following depletion of HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP, chromosomes did not congress, and chromosomes and spindle poles separated prematurely 40 s after NEBD concomitant with sister chromatid co-segregation towards the same spindle pole (Figure 1B–H; Video 1) (Cheeseman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 1B-H and Video 1.

claim: Early pole and chromosome separation in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP is not caused by premature anaphase onset.
source: This early pole and chromosome separation was not caused by premature anaphase onset, as the fluorescent signal of a Separase activation sensor remained on chromosomes well after they completed separation in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E) (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: A vast majority of chromosomes remain mono-oriented in HCP-1/2CENP-F- or CLS-2CLASP-depleted zygotes.
source: Instead, a vast majority of chromosomes remained mono-oriented in HCP-1/2CENP-F- or CLS-2CLASP-depleted zygotes (Figure 1F–H) (Cheeseman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 1F-H.

claim: Sister chromatid co-segregation in HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP depletion is due to improperly mono-oriented chromosomes rather than premature mitotic exit.
source: This indicates that the sister chromatid co-segregation phenotype resulting from depletion of HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP is due to improperly mono-oriented chromosomes rather than premature mitotic exit.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1 depletion restores biorientation and rescues the sister chromatid segregation failure typical of CLS-2CLASP depletion.
source: Strikingly BUB-1 depletion restored biorientation and rescued the sister chromatid segregation failure typical of CLS-2CLASP depletion (Figure 1B,C; Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1B,C and Video 1.

claim: BUB-1 depletion rescues sister chromatid segregation in Δhcp-2 mutants co-depleted of HCP-1CENP-F.
source: We also observed similar sister chromatid segregation rescue by co-depleting BUB-1 and HCP-1CENP-F or HCP-2CENP-F, in CRIPSR-cas9 generated hcp-2 (Δhcp-2) (Figure 1B,C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C) and hcp-1 (Δhcp-1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–E) deletion mutants respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: BUB-1 and HCP-1CENP-F (or HCP-2CENP-F) co-depleted embryos display delayed congression and merotelic attachments.
source: BUB-1 and HCP-1CENP-F (or HCP-2CENP-F) co-depleted embryos displayed a 'BUB-1-like' phenotype with delayed congression (Figure 1B,C) and merotelic attachments to both spindle poles evidenced by bent kinetochores during metaphase and kinetochore stretches during anaphase (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1B,C and Figure 1F-H.

claim: BUB-1 prevents chromosome biorientation, and this activity is revealed in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP.
source: Together, these results suggest that BUB-1 prevents chromosome biorientation, and that this activity is revealed in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1 recruitment to kinetochores depends on phosphorylated MELT repeats located in the N-terminal part of KNL-1.
source: BUB-1 recruitment to kinetochores depends on phosphorylated MELT repeats located in the N-terminal part of the kinetochore scaffolding protein KNL-1 (Vleugel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: KNL-1Δ85-505 lacks all MELT repeats and abolishes BUB-1 recruitment to kinetochores.
source: To abolish BUB-1 recruitment to kinetochores, we used a C. elegans strain expressing a truncation mutant of KNL-1 (KNL-1Δ85-505), which lacks all MELT repeats (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) (Moyle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the presence of KNL-1Δ85-505, co-depleted zygotes display delayed congression and bioriented merotelic attachments.
source: In contrast, in the presence of KNL-1Δ85-505, and therefore in the absence of BUB-1 at kinetochores (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), co-depleted zygotes displayed a 'BUB-1-like' phenotype with delayed congression and bioriented merotelic attachments (Figure 2B–D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2B-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: BUB-1 inhibitory activity on biorientation depends on its kinetochore localisation.
source: Together, these results show that BUB-1 inhibitory activity on biorientation depends on its kinetochore localisation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1ΔKD and BUB-1K718R;D847N, but not BUB-1D814N, lead to delayed anaphase onset.
source: In line with previous findings on BUB-1 function in the regulation of anaphase onset, BUB-1ΔKD and BUB-1K718R ;D847N, but not BUB-1D814N, led to delayed anaphase onset (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B) (Kim et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: All BUB-1 mutants (BUB-1ΔKD, BUB-1K718R;D847N, BUB-1D814N) localize to kinetochores in absence of endogenous BUB-1.
source: Importantly, all of these mCherry-tagged mutants localised to kinetochores in absence of endogenous BUB-1, allowing us to test their influence on kinetochore-microtubule attachments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: BUB-1ΔKD prevents HCP-1CENP-F kinetochore localization.
source: Interestingly, BUB-1ΔKD prevented HCP-1CENP-F kinetochore localization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: BUB1 recruitment of CENP-F via its kinase domain is conserved from humans to C. elegans.
source: suggesting that BUB1 recruitment of CENP-F via its kinase domain is conserved from humans to C. elegans (Ciossani et al., 2018; Raaijmakers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: The presence of mainly bioriented chromosomes with amphitelic attachments in BUB-1ΔKD mutant suggests that BUB-1's inhibitory role during biorientation is dependent on the kinase domain.
source: Furthermore, the presence of mainly bioriented chromosomes with amphitelic attachments in this mutant that lacks kinetochore HCP-1/2CENP-F, suggests that BUB-1's inhibitory role during biorientation is dependent on the kinase domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1ΔKD and BUB-1K718R;D847N attenuate the HCP-1/2CENP-F loss-of-function phenotype, allowing delayed but successful chromosome congression and biorientation with merotelic attachments.
source: In contrast, the phenotype was attenuated with BUB-1ΔKD and BUB-1K718R ;D847N: chromosome congression was delayed but occurred successfully (Figure 3B,C; Video 3), and chromosome biorientation with merotelic attachments was established (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3B-D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The appearance of merotelic attachments only after depletion of HCP-1/2CENP-F in BUB-1ΔKD suggests that HCP-1/2CENP-F promote non-merotelic attachments independently of its kinetochore localization.
source: The appearance of a large proportion of merotelic attachments only after depletion of HCP-1/2CENP-F in BUB-1ΔKD (which normally lacks kinetochore-associated HCP-1/2CENP-F) suggests that HCP-1/2CENP-F promote non-merotelic attachments independently of its kinetochore localization (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The integrity of the kinase domain is required for BUB-1 inhibition of chromosome congression and biorientation.
source: Furthermore, these results confirm that the integrity of the kinase domain is required for BUB-1 inhibition of chromosome congression and biorientation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The HCP-1/2CENP-F loss-of-function phenotype is not rescued by BUB-1D814N, which specifically disrupts the kinase activity.
source: In contrast, the HCP-1/2CENP-F loss-of-function phenotype was not rescued by BUB-1D814N, which specifically disrupts the kinase activity (Figure 3B–D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) (Moyle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 3B-D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: BUB-1's inhibitory role on biorientation depends on its kinase domain, but not its kinase activity.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that BUB-1's inhibitory role on biorientation depends on its kinase domain, but not its kinase activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: In mammals, BUB1 contributes to recruiting the RZZ complex, and thus probably also dynein-dynactin, to kinetochores.
source: In mammals, BUB1 contributes to recruiting the RZZ complex, and thus probably also dynein-dynactin, to kinetochores (Caldas et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: BUB-1 depletion leads to a drastic reduction of ZWL-1Zwilch at kinetochores.
source: Consistent with previous results in human cells, BUB-1 depletion led to a drastic reduction of the GFP-tagged RZZ complex component ZWL-1Zwilch at kinetochores (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: BUB-1 depletion leads to complete loss of DNC-2p50 from kinetochores.
source: Reduction in RZZ kinetochore targeting coincided with the complete loss of the GFP-tagged dynactin subunit DNC-2p50 from kinetochores, which instead localized diffusely on chromosomes and in the spindle region (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: BUB-1 is required for dynein-dynactin recruitment to kinetochores in C. elegans zygotes.
source: Therefore BUB-1 is required for dynein-dynactin recruitment to kinetochores in C. elegans zygotes, and the residual pool of RZZ complex that localises to kinetochores independently of BUB-1 does not contribute to dynein-dynactin recruitment.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Both ZWL-1Zwilch and DNC-2p50 are present at kinetochores in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F.
source: Importantly, both ZWL-1Zwilch and DNC-2p50 were present at kinetochores in absence of HCP-1/2 CENP-F (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Co-depletion of ZWL-1Zwilch with HCP-1CENP-F leads to slight improvement in chromosome congression, and chromosome segregation occurs later and more slowly than in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F alone.
source: For this, we co-depleted ZWL-1Zwilch with HCP-1CENP-F in the Δhcp-2 strain. This led to a slight improvement in chromosome congression, and chromosome segregation occurred later and more slowly than in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F alone (Figure 4C,D; Video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4C,D and Video 4.

claim: RZZ and dynein promote rapid end-on attachments and early co-segregation of sister chromatids in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F.
source: This result suggests that RZZ and dynein promote rapid end-on attachments and early co-segregation of sister chromatids in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Chromosome biorientation is not restored and sister chromatids still co-segregate upon co-depletion of ZWL-1Zwilch and HCP-1/2CENP-F.
source: However, chromosome biorientation was not restored and sister chromatid still co-segregated in this condition (Figure 4C–E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E; Video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4C-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: BUB-1ΔKD mutant supports normal recruitment of DNC-2p50 but does not inhibit chromosome biorientation in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F.
source: Further evidence confirming the independence of BUB-1 activities in inhibiting chromosome biorientation and in recruiting RZZ and dynein-dynactin came from our analysis of the BUB-1ΔKD mutant, which could support the normal recruitment of DNC-2p50 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) but did not inhibit chromosome biorientation in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and Figure 3B-D.

claim: Kinetochore recruitment of RZZ and dynein-dynactin by BUB-1 is important for initial end-on attachments, but does not explain BUB-1 inhibition of chromosome biorientation.
source: Therefore, kinetochore recruitment of RZZ and dynein-dynactin by BUB-1 is important for initial end-on attachments, but does not explain BUB-1 inhibition of chromosome biorientation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1ΔKD mutant leads to a decreased frequency of merotelic attachments and reduced kinetochore stretches in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F.
source: However, in contrast to the full BUB-1 depletion, the BUB-1ΔKD mutant also led to a decreased frequency of merotelic attachments (Figures 3D and 4E) and reduced kinetochore stretches in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figures 3D, 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The high degree of merotely observed upon BUB-1 codepletion with HCP-1/2CENP-F is largely caused by the loss of dynein from kinetochores.
source: This suggests that the high degree of merotely observed upon BUB-1 codepletion with HCP-1/2CENP-F is largely caused by the loss of dynein from kinetochores, and that BUB-1 favours amphitelic attachments by recruiting dynein to kinetochores.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1 favours amphitelic attachments by recruiting dynein to kinetochores.
source: This suggests that the high degree of merotely observed upon BUB-1 codepletion with HCP-1/2CENP-F is largely caused by the loss of dynein from kinetochores, and that BUB-1 favours amphitelic attachments by recruiting dynein to kinetochores.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Recruiting the RZZ complex and dynein-dynactin at the kinetochore is a critical function of BUB-1 to promote amphitelic end-on attachments.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that recruiting the RZZ complex and dynein-dynactin at the kinetochore is a critical function of BUB-1 to promote amphitelic end-on attachments (Gassmann et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1 inhibits chromosome congression and biorientation independently of AIR-2Aurora B activity.
source: Upon upshift of HCP-1/2CENP-F-depleted air-2(ts) mutant embryos to the restrictive temperature, sister chromatids still co-segregated prematurely (100 s after NEBD). Therefore BUB-1 inhibits chromosome congression and biorientation independently of AIR-2Aurora B activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: GFP-tagged SKA-1 is undetectable at kinetochores in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F.
source: Accordingly, we found that GFP-tagged SKA-1 was undetectable at kinetochores in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: SKA-1 kinetochore localization depends on the tension exerted at kinetochores by end-on attachments.
source: However, as SKA-1 kinetochore localization depends on the tension exerted at kinetochores by end-on attachments (Cheerambathur et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Mono-oriented attachments in ZYG-1Plk4-depleted 2 cell stage embryos provide sufficient tension for SKA complex kinetochore localization.
source: In this condition, SKA-1::GFP accumulated on the chromosome side that faces the spindle monopole, demonstrating that mono-oriented attachments in ZYG-1Plk4-depleted 2 cell stage embryos provide sufficient tension for SKA complex kinetochore localization (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,C.

claim: SKA-1 kinetochore recruitment is inhibited in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F, but the mono-oriented attachment configuration is not sufficient to account for the lack of kinetochore SKA-1.
source: Together, these results suggest that SKA-1 kinetochore recruitment is inhibited in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F, but that the mono-oriented attachment configuration is not sufficient to account for the lack of kinetochore SKA-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: SKA-1::GFP kinetochore recruitment is rescued by depleting BUB-1 in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F.
source: Most importantly, SKA-1::GFP kinetochore recruitment was rescued by depleting BUB-1 in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: BUB-1 prevents SKA-1 recruitment to kinetochores when HCP-1/2CENP-F is absent.
source: suggesting that BUB-1 prevents SKA-1 recruitment to kinetochores when HCP-1/2CENP-F is absent.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Both BUB-1ΔKD and BUB-1K718R;D847N mutants allow kinetochore recruitment of SKA-1::GFP.
source: In agreement with our first prediction, both mutants allowed kinetochore recruitment of SKA-1::GFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2F.

claim: In the simultaneous absence of endogenous BUB-1, HCP-1/2CENP-F and SKA-1, both BUB-1ΔKD and BUB-1K718R;D847N mutants lead to complete failure of chromosome congression and biorientation.
source: Strikingly in the simultaneous absence of endogenous BUB-1, HCP-1/2CENP-F and SKA-1, both BUB-1 mutants (BUB-1ΔKD and BUB-1K718R ;D847N) led to complete failure of chromosome congression and biorientation, along with sister chromatid co-segregation, similar to what is observed after HCP-1/2CENP-F depletion alone (Figure 5C–E; Figure 5—figure supplement 2G; Video 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5C-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2G.

claim: BUB-1ΔKD and BUB-1K718R;D847N are capable of sustaining chromosome biorientation in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F only when the SKA complex is present.
source: Thus BUB-1ΔKD and BUB-1K718R ;D847N are capable of sustaining chromosome biorientation in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F only when the SKA complex is present.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: In BUB-1ΔKD and BUB-1K718R;D847N mutants, the kinetochore-localized SKA complex is responsible for the observed rescue of chromosome biorientation in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F.
source: This result suggests that in these two BUB-1 mutants the kinetochore-localized SKA complex is responsible for the observed rescue of chromosome biorientation in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: In absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP, BUB-1 inhibits stable biorientation of chromosomes by preventing SKA complex recruitment to kinetochores.
source: Altogether, our results suggest that, in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP, BUB-1 inhibits stable biorientation of chromosomes by preventing SKA complex recruitment to kinetochores (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The phenotype of premature sister chromatid co-segregation upon loss of CLS-2CLASP can be rescued by alleviating BUB-1-mediated inhibition of SKA-1 at the kinetochores.
source: We found that this phenotype can be rescued by alleviating BUB-1-mediated inhibition of SKA-1 at the kinetochores, preventing SKA-mediated attachment maturation.
evidence: This is stated in the results and is based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The capacity for chromosomes to engage in stable connections to both spindle poles can be provided either by efficient kinetochore microtubule polymerization or by kinetochore-microtubule attachment maturation.
source: These observations suggest that the capacity for chromosomes to engage in stable connections to both spindle poles can be provided either by efficient kinetochore microtubule polymerization or by kinetochore-microtubule attachment maturation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1 provides two opposing activities in the establishment of bioriented amphitelic connections: promoting biorientation by recruiting CLS-2CLASP to kinetochores, and restricting biorientation by limiting SKA-mediated attachment maturation.
source: Thus, BUB-1 provides two opposing activities in the establishment of bioriented amphitelic connections: (1) promoting biorientation by recruiting CLS-2CLASP to kinetochores, and (2) restricting biorientation by limiting SKA-mediated attachment maturation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Embryos expressing BUB-1ΔKD only present slight merotely at 24°C, but lowering the temperature to 15°C raises the rate of merotely by three-fold.
source: Embryos expressing BUB-1ΔKD only presented slight merotely at 24°C, but lowering the temperature down to 15°C, and therefore lowering overall microtubule growth (Srayko et al., 2005), raised this rate of merotely by three-fold (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A similar temperature dependency for embryonic lethality is observed in the BUB-1ΔKD mutant.
source: We observed a similar temperature dependency for embryonic lethality in this mutant (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Promoting kinetochore microtubule assembly via BUB-1-mediated recruitment of CLS-2CLASP is required to avoid merotely and embryonic lethality.
source: These results suggest that promoting kinetochore microtubule assembly via BUB-1-mediated recruitment of CLS-2CLASP is required to avoid merotely and embryonic lethality.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1K718R;D847N mutant-expressing embryos display up to 21% embryonic lethality when raised at 24°C.
source: In contrast to control BUB-1WT-expressing embryos, we found that BUB-1K718R ;D847N mutant-expressing embryos displayed up to 21% embryonic lethality when raised at 24°C.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Embryos depleted of MDF-1Mad1 do not show the same temperature-dependent lethality as BUB-1K718R;D847N mutant embryos.
source: Embryos depleted of the SAC protein MDF-1Mad1 did not show the same temperature-dependent lethality (8%), nor did the BUB-1D814N mutant (3.4%).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The BUB-1K718R;D847N mutant phenotype is not caused by a defective SAC or a lack of BUB-1 kinase activity, but rather by the enhanced microtubule growth at high temperature.
source: The BUB-1K718R ;D847N mutant phenotype is therefore not caused by a defective SAC or a lack of BUB-1 kinase activity, but rather by the enhanced microtubule growth at high temperature (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: When load-bearing connections are favoured by high microtubule dynamics, limiting SKA-mediated attachment maturation becomes essential.
source: In other words, when load-bearing connections are favoured by high microtubule dynamics, limiting SKA-mediated attachment maturation becomes essential.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1 displays opposing activities at the kinetochore to promote properly bioriented kinetochore-microtubule attachments and to prevent embryonic lethality.
source: Together, our data suggest that BUB-1 displays opposing activities at the kinetochore to promote properly bioriented kinetochore-microtubule attachments and to prevent embryonic lethality.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1 has two previously uncharacterized functions: accelerating end-on kinetochore-microtubule attachments by recruiting the dynein-dynactin complex to kinetochores, and limiting attachment maturation by the SKA complex.
source: Here, we identify two previously uncharacterized functions of the C. elegans BUB-1 kinase in (1) accelerating end-on kinetochore-microtubule attachments by recruiting the dynein-dynactin complex to kinetochores, and (2) limiting attachment maturation by the SKA complex (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is a summary of the primary findings.

claim: BUB-1's activity in limiting attachment maturation by the SKA complex relies on the BUB-1 kinase domain but is independent of kinase activity.
source: We show this latter activity relies on the BUB-1 kinase domain but is independent of kinase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on the experimental data presented.

claim: C. elegans BUB-1 targets HCP-1/2CENP-F to kinetochores, which in turn recruit CLS-2CLASP.
source: Previously, C. elegans BUB-1 was shown to target the two redundant CENP-F orthologs HCP-1/2CENP-F to kinetochores, which in turn recruit the CLASP protein CLS-2CLASP (Cheeseman et al., 2005; Encalada et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: CLASP at kinetochores promotes microtubule assembly and increases microtubule dynamics, favouring amphitelic attachments.
source: CLASP at kinetochores promotes microtubule assembly and increases microtubule dynamics, favouring amphitelic attachments (Maffini et al., 2009; Maiato et al., 2003a; Maiato et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: BUB-1 both promotes amphitely through the RZZ-dynein-dynactin complex and CLS-2CLASP, while limiting maturation of chromosome biorientation by the SKA complex.
source: Therefore, our results show that BUB-1 both promotes amphitely through the RZZ-dynein-dynactin complex and CLS-2CLASP, while limiting maturation of chromosome biorientation by the SKA complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The coordination of BUB-1's different activities is required to avoid merotely and embryonic lethality.
source: Our data also suggest that the coordination of these different activities by BUB-1 is required to avoid merotely and embryonic lethality.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1 has a central role in promoting accurate chromosome biorientation essential to maintain genetic integrity during cell division.
source: These results therefore define a central role for BUB-1 in promoting accurate chromosome biorientation essential to maintain genetic integrity during cell division.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1 contributes to kinetochore recruitment of the RZZ complex in C. elegans, which is essential to avoid merotely.
source: Here, we show that in C. elegans, BUB-1 also contributes to kinetochore recruitment of the RZZ complex and that this is essential to avoid merotely.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Some RZZ remains at kinetochores following BUB1 depletion in human cells, suggesting an additional kinetochore-binding site must exist.
source: In human cells, some RZZ remains at kinetochores following BUB1 depletion, which suggests an additional kinetochore-binding site must exist.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on knowledge from the literature.

claim: Zwint was originally proposed to be the primary kinetochore-docking partner of RZZ in human cells.
source: The kinetochore protein Zwint, which interacts with the KNL1 C-terminal half, was originally proposed to be the primary kinetochore-docking partner of RZZ in human cells (Kops et al., 2005; Petrovic et al., 2010; Starr et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Some RZZ remains at kinetochores in human cells even in absence of KNL1 and BUB1.
source: However, some RZZ remains at kinetochores in human cells even in absence of KNL1 (and thus also in absence of kinetochore-localized Zwint) and BUB1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on knowledge from the literature.

claim: The distant Zwint ortholog KBP-5 is dispensable for RZZ kinetochore recruitment in C. elegans.
source: Consistently, the distant Zwint ortholog KBP-5 is dispensable for RZZ kinetochore recruitment in C. elegans (Varma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: A Zwint-, KNL1- and BUB1-independent pathway has been hypothesized to participate in RZZ localization at human kinetochores.
source: A Zwint-, KNL1- and BUB1-independent pathway has therefore been hypothesized to participate in RZZ localization at human kinetochores (Caldas et al., 2015; Silió et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: BUB-1 depletion does not fully abrogate kinetochore RZZ localization.
source: Although the molecular details of this alternative contact site between RZZ and the kinetochore are still unclear, our results are consistent with this hypothesis, as BUB-1 depletion does not fully abrogate kinetochore RZZ localization (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1 is absolutely required for dynein-dynactin recruitment to kinetochores.
source: In contrast, we found that BUB-1 is absolutely required for dynein-dynactin recruitment to kinetochores.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1 downstream partners HCP-1/2CENP-F recruit NUD-2NudE/el to stabilise dynein-dynactin at kinetochores.
source: One potential explanation for the apparent discrepancy between this complete lack of dynein-dynactin at kinetochores despite partial recruitment of the RZZ complex may stem from BUB-1 downstream partners HCP-1/2CENP-F, which recruit NUD-2NudE/el to stabilise dynein-dynactin at kinetochores (Simões et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: BUB-1 would both recruit dynein-dynactin via the RZZ complex, and stabilise it at kinetochores via HCP-1/2CENP-F and NUD-2NudE/el.
source: BUB-1 would therefore both recruit dynein-dynactin via the RZZ complex, and stabilise it at kinetochores via HCP-1/2CENP-F and NUD-2NudE/el.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the experimental data and literature.

claim: Both BUB-1-mediated RZZ and dynein-dynactin recruitments contribute to accelerating the establishment of end-on attachments and to the prevention of merotely.
source: Our functional analysis comparing BUB-1-depleted embryos in the presence or absence of the BUB-1ΔKD mutant, which recruits DNC-2p50 normally to kinetochores (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), shows that both BUB-1-mediated RZZ and dynein-dynactin recruitments contribute to accelerating the establishment of end-on attachments and to the prevention of merotely (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on the experimental data presented.

claim: RZZ and dynein-dynactin constitute a kinetochore module, recruited downstream of BUB-1, that contributes to rapidly and accurately establishing biorientation in early mitosis.
source: RZZ and dynein-dynactin therefore constitute a kinetochore module, recruited downstream of BUB-1, that contributes to rapidly and accurately establishing biorientation in early mitosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: In C. elegans zygotes, BUB-1 targets HCP-1/2CENP-F to kinetochores, which in turn recruits CLS-2CLASP.
source: In C. elegans zygotes, BUB-1 targets HCP-1/2CENP-F to kinetochores, which in turn recruits CLS-2CLASP (Cheeseman et al., 2005; Encalada et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Kinetochore-localized CLS-2CLASP is thought to promote microtubule polymerization essential for proper chromosome biorientation.
source: Kinetochore-localized CLS-2CLASP is thought to promote microtubule polymerization essential for proper chromosome biorientation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on knowledge from the literature.

claim: Upon HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP depletion, chromosomes become bioriented only when kinetochore-localized BUB-1 is absent.
source: Our work stresses the importance of BUB-1 in antagonizing CLS-2CLASP-dependent kinetochore microtubule assembly by limiting their attachment to kinetochores. We indeed found that upon HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP depletion, chromosomes become bioriented only when kinetochore-localized BUB-1 is absent.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1 limits kinetochore-microtubule attachment maturation by preventing SKA complex kinetochore recruitment.
source: Our results further suggest that BUB-1 limits kinetochore-microtubule attachment maturation by preventing SKA complex kinetochore recruitment.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1 could indirectly regulate the interaction between the SKA complex and NDC-80 by recruiting Aurora A at the kinetochore.
source: Second, BUB-1 could indirectly regulate the interaction between the SKA complex and its kinetochore docking partner NDC-80, by recruiting Aurora A at the kinetochore.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculative possibility.

claim: In human cells, BUB1 recruits Aurora A at the centromere, where it phosphorylates the NDC80 tail.
source: Indeed, although Aurora B-dependent phosphorylation of the NDC-80 tail prevents enrichment of the SKA complex at kinetochores in C. elegans (Cheerambathur et al., 2017), we rule out here a role for Aurora B as a mediator of BUB-1 inhibition of biorientation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). In contrast, in human cells, BUB1 was recently shown to recruit Aurora A at the centromere (Eot-Houllier et al., 2018), where it phosphorylates the NDC80 tail (DeLuca et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: BUB-1 could directly or indirectly decrease tension at kinetochores.
source: Finally, BUB-1 could directly or indirectly decrease tension at kinetochores.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculative possibility.

claim: In C. elegans, kinetochore tension has been proposed to promote SKA complex recruitment.
source: In C. elegans, kinetochore tension has been proposed to promote SKA complex recruitment (Cheerambathur et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Monopolar spindles are compatible with normal level of SKA complex at kinetochores.
source: We showed that monopolar spindles, in which kinetochore tension is likely low, are compatible with normal level of SKA complex at kinetochores.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Mono-oriented chromosomes, as visible in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP, could potentially display even lower kinetochore tension, which would abrogate SKA complex kinetochore localization.
source: However, mono-oriented chromosomes, as visible in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP, could potentially display even lower kinetochore tension, which would abrogate SKA complex kinetochore localization.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculative possibility.

claim: By increasing tension at kinetochores through an unknown mechanism, BUB-1 could restore SKA complex kinetochore enrichment and chromosome biorientation.
source: By increasing tension at kinetochores through an unknown mechanism, BUB-1 could restore SKA complex kinetochore enrichment and chromosome biorientation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculative possibility.

claim: Hyper-recruitment of SKA-1 to kinetochores is not observed in the absence of BUB-1.
source: Regardless of the exact mechanism by which BUB-1 regulates the SKA complex, we surprisingly did not observe hyper-recruitment of SKA-1 to kinetochores in the absence of BUB-1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B), nor in the presence of BUB-1 mutants that do not inhibit chromosome biorientation in absence of HCP-1/2CENP-F (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Upon depletion of HCP-1/2CENP-F, BUB-1 is hyper-recruited to kinetochores.
source: However, upon depletion of HCP-1/2CENP-F (proteins dependent upon BUB-1 for kinetochore localisation, Figure 1E), when SKA complex kinetochore recruitment is inhibited, BUB-1 is hyper-recruited to kinetochores (Figure 5—figure supplement 2H,I).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on the experimental data presented.

claim: A threshold level of BUB-1 could be required to prevent SKA complex localization at kinetochores.
source: Although the reason for this hyper-recruitment is unclear, it suggests that a threshold level of BUB-1 could be required to prevent SKA complex localization at kinetochores.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculative possibility based on the experimental data.

claim: Depleting HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP would amplify the BUB-1-mediated inhibition of SKA complex kinetochore localization.
source: In this context, depleting HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP would therefore amplify the BUB-1-mediated inhibition of SKA complex kinetochore localization, which in the C. elegans embryo is otherwise not apparent and probably extremely transient during prometaphase when biorientation is established.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculative possibility based on the experimental data.

claim: The embryonic lethality observed in the BUB-1K718R,D847N mutant at high temperature (21% at 24°C) demonstrates the essential and physiological role of BUB-1 in restricting biorientation.
source: Nevertheless, the embryonic lethality observed in the BUB-1K718R,D847N mutant incapable of restricting biorientation (but which recruits HCP-1/2CENP-F and CLS-2CLASP at kinetochores) at high temperature (21% at 24°C) demonstrates the essential and physiological role of this pathway (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1 is a key regulator of the kinetochore-microtubule interface that facilitates amphitelic kinetochore-microtubule attachments and shields chromosomes from merotely.
source: Our study provides mechanistic insights into the non-SAC role for BUB-1 in chromosome segregation, suggesting it is a key regulator of the kinetochore-microtubule interface that facilitates amphitelic kinetochore-microtubule attachments and shields chromosomes from merotely.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BUB-1 dependent recruitment of the RZZ complex and of dynein-dynactin favours initial end-on kinetochore-microtubule attachments in bioriented conformations.
source: In this model, BUB-1 dependent recruitment of the RZZ complex and of dynein-dynactin favours initial end-on kinetochore-microtubule attachments in bioriented conformations.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as part of a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: BUB-1 controls the stability of attachments through two opposing activities: favouring NDC-80-mediated load-bearing attachments via recruitment of HCP-1/2CENP-F and CLS-2CLASP, and limiting attachment maturation by preventing SKA complex kinetochore targeting.
source: BUB-1 then controls the stability of these attachments through two opposing activities. First, BUB-1 favours NDC-80-mediated load-bearing attachments via recruitment of HCP-1/2CENP-F and CLS-2CLASP, which promote kinetochore microtubule assembly. Second BUB-1 limits attachment maturation by preventing SKA complex kinetochore targeting.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as part of a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: BUB-1 activities help establish amphitelic attachments and prevent errors in chromosome segregation.
source: Together these activities help establishing amphitelic attachments and preventing errors in chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as part of a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: BUB-1 progressively leaves from kinetochores in metaphase, allowing SKA complex accumulation and kinetochore microtubule attachment maturation.
source: BUB-1 then progressively leaves from kinetochores in metaphase (Figure 6D; Figure 5—figure supplement 2H,I), allowing SKA complex accumulation and kinetochore microtubule attachment maturation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as part of a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: The high frequency of embryonic lethality in C. elegans zygotes in the presence of BUB-1 mutants that uncouple BUB-1's two functions stresses the importance of coordinating temporally kinetochore microtubule initial attachments and their maturation.
source: The high frequency of embryonic lethality observed in C. elegans zygotes in the presence of BUB-1 mutants that uncouple these two functions (BUB-1ΔKD or BUB-1K718R ;D847N), stresses the importance of coordinating temporally kinetochore microtubule initial attachments and their maturation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: BUB-1's non-SAC role in limiting SKA-mediated attachment maturation is revealed when HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP is deficient.
source: In conclusion, using the C. elegans model, we reveal a non-SAC role for BUB-1 in limiting SKA-mediated attachment maturation, when HCP-1/2CENP-F or CLS-2CLASP is deficient.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: BUB-1-mediated inhibition of chromosome biorientation is linked to its kinase domain, but not to the kinase activity.
source: Indeed, we found that BUB-1-mediated inhibition of chromosome biorientation is linked to its kinase domain, but not to the kinase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The yet unidentified BUB1-dependent activity that prevents lethality of SAC-deficient haploid HAP1 human cells is also linked to the kinase domain but not the kinase activity.
source: This is also the case for the yet unidentified BUB1-dependent activity that prevents lethality of SAC-deficient haploid HAP1 human cells (Raaijmakers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The conservation of all the key molecular players suggests the non-SAC role for BUB-1 in regulating kinetochore-microtubule attachments could be a general and conserved function of BUB1 in metazoans.
source: The conservation of all the key molecular players suggests this non-SAC role for BUB-1 in regulating kinetochore-microtubule attachments could be a general and conserved function of BUB1 in metazoans.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculative conclusion based on the experimental data and knowledge.

claim: Kinetochores are holocentric in the C. elegans nematode and form along the length of sister chromatids.
source: Kinetochores are holocentric in the C. elegans nematode and form along the length of sister chromatids (Dernburg, 2001)
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: In C. elegans zygotes, spindle pole separation is primarily driven by cortical pulling forces transmitted through astral microtubules.
source: In C. elegans zygotes, spindle pole separation is primarily driven by cortical pulling forces transmitted through astral microtubules (Grill et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Cortical forces are opposed by load-bearing connections between bioriented chromosomes and the two poles of the mitotic spindle.
source: Cortical forces are then opposed by load-bearing connections between bioriented chromosomes and the two poles of the mitotic spindle.
evidence: This is stated in the results and is based on knowledge from the literature.

claim: Spindle elongation (pole to pole distance) over time is used as an indirect read-out of load-bearing connections.
source: We therefore also measured spindle elongation (pole to pole distance) over time as an indirect read-out of these connections (Figure 1A,C) (Desai et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.
